orbit: Governing MCP for a workforce the size of a city.
So how many people are using MCP in this workforce? Let me put it in ships.
An Enterprise's worth: four hundred and twenty-eight?
The Executor, two hundred and eighty thousand?
The Death Star, one point two million?
I am not supposed to say the exact number. But it is about two-thirds of a Death Star, actively using MCP every single day.
expected: You might think I am going to do a technical keynote. We are at a tech conference. But my message today is remarkably untechnical.
You expect the number, the architecture, the process, the security issues, and the things we thought were unusual.
People have covered those all week, and it is all on the website.
What I really want you to leave with is the most effective lever for MCP adoption. It was not what I expected. Before that, the things you expect.
city: The architecture, the simple version. A person. A device. An agent running on that device. One gate, a proxy and a registry, that every tool call goes through. And the tools behind it.
Done properly: the managed device with its policies, tool traffic through the proxy and the gateway, model traffic through its own gateway, and the control plane feeding all of it.
Now look at the two red dashed lines at the bottom. The shell and the browser never touch any of it. Hold that thought.
gates: Our process for accepting a server: six gates.
Do we have a relationship with the vendor?
Is there a real business need?
Is it well built, and wrapped where it falls short?
Does it speak the current spec?
Does it meet our security standards?
The complete checklist, with every source, is on the site.
attack: One security tale that surprised us. CVE-2026-47250. One line in a log file.
An operator asks the agent to read the logs, and it feeds the planted instruction to the agent along with everything else.
The agent runs kubectl against the attacker's server, with TLS verification switched off.
kubectl sends the operator's bearer token with the request.
The attacker now holds a token for a cluster they could not reach.
A hacker's game is multi-dimensional chess: gather everything now, and the day that cluster is exposed, they have one more piece.
wrapped: And things we thought were unusual. We wrapped MCP servers in MCP servers, and we thought that was weird. Apparently everybody is doing it.
The server does not meet our security standards.
Credentials must not cross from client to server.
A hundred tools offered, and nine presented.
Reads and writes split into separate servers.
The full list, and the tools, are on the site.
whatif: But it is not the architecture or the gating process I really want to talk about. What if you gave your end users generative AI, and MCP,
and said: plug them in like USB, sprinkle them everywhere like your favorite hot sauce, and relentlessly use AI, because that is how we win?
You handed everyone a relentless hacker, on your hardware, inside your security zones, with your AI accounts and your tools.
And it runs on the end-user device, authenticated as that user. People forget that a laptop is a server.
So what happens when you tell people with superpowers no?
theno: Then the user made a reasonable request. I want a tool that reads my mail. No problem.
Draft replies for me? Not entirely comfortable, but fine.
Send email as me? Whoa. Hold on.
These are human tools for human communication. A bot has to be labeled as a bot, secured as a bot, given its own identity. Nobody has solved that yet.
So we said no, and we offered alternatives.
And the user asked the agent: I do not see an MCP server for Outlook. Is there some other way we might do this?
sayno: The agent wrote PowerShell. Classic Outlook has had an automation interface for decades, and on a healthy, managed laptop the script went straight through. It read and sent mail as the user.

Then they asked about Teams. We said no again. So they put the approved browser in remote debugging mode, and the agent walked the browser, and the browser walked Teams. It never opened Teams. It opened a browser.
Remember the two red dashed lines? The shell and the browser never touch the gate.
lever: So what was the biggest lever? The policy? The architecture? The proxies, the registries? None of that alone.

We had to win the hearts and minds of users, because for the first time an internal team is a SaaS company, and its biggest threat is its own end users. If you do not get their buy-in, they ask the agent to do it. That is how you get shadow IT.
So love your users. Figure out what they need, and get them to yes.
Say no when you must, and explain why. A no without a why is a workaround waiting to happen.
Send the signals: let them vote, let them ask, let them tell you where the openings are.
And run the service like a product: a self-service form, a feedback path, a leaderboard, communities of practice, done relentlessly.
close: The architecture, the policies, the process: yes, all of that. But the biggest lever is a relationship with the users who consume your MCP servers.
Talk and listen. It is not just a technology problem. More than ever it is a human problem, and humans can help us solve it.
The details are at mcp dot michael rishi forrester dot com. Come find me.
